questions.q: Is it true that sequential algorithms (consisting only of a linear chain of commands) are capable of solving absolutely any computational problem in programming?
questions.hint: Think about whether it is possible to find, for example, the maximum of two numbers without conditions and choices.
options: True
False
explanations: Incorrect. Simple linear sequences of instructions cannot solve problems where the choice of action depends on the input data. This requires selection/branching structures.
Correct! Solving most real-world problems requires more complex control structures, such as selection (branching).

questions.topic: Branching — Signature of the main Function
questions.q: What will happen when compiling code main() { ... } without specifying the int signature before main() in modern C standards (C99 and newer)?
questions.hint: Recall the implicit int rules in older and modern C standards.
options: In older standards (C89/C90) this will compile due to implicit int, but in C99+ it will cause a compiler warning or error
This is a syntax error forbidden in absolutely all C standards
The compiler will automatically insert void instead of int
The program will compile without any warnings in all standards
explanations: Correct! In the old C89 standard, an omitted return type defaulted to `int`, but starting from C99 the 'implicit int' rule was completely removed from the language.
Incorrect. In the C89/C90 standard, omitting `int` before `main()` was permitted.
Incorrect. The compiler does not insert `void`; previously `int` was inserted by default.
Incorrect. Starting from C99, the absence of a return type leads to a compiler error or warning.

questions.q: Which if statement does the else keyword belong to in the widget code (in the absence of curly braces)?
questions.hint: Consider the rule for binding an else branch to preceding if statements in C.
options: To the second (nested) if (x > 0)
To the first (outer) if (a > 0)
The compiler will issue an error due to ambiguity
The else branch will be ignored by the compiler
explanations: Correct! In C, an `else` branch is always associated with the nearest preceding `if` statement that does not already have an `else` pair (unless an explicit `{}` block specifies a different scope).
Incorrect. Despite indentation, the compiler binds `else` to the nearest `if (x > 0)`.
Incorrect. There is no ambiguity for the compiler, as the rule unambiguously binds `else` to the nearest `if`.
Incorrect. The `else` branch compiles fully and binds to the inner `if`.

questions.topic: Branching — Assignment Error = Instead of Comparison ==
questions.q: What will happen when executing the code shown in the widget, where the condition contains x = y instead of x == y?
questions.hint: Recall what value the assignment operator = returns in C and how it is interpreted as a logical condition.
options: The value of y (5) will be assigned to x, the condition will become true (>0), and "Equal" will be printed
The compiler will issue an error and forbid the `=` operation inside `if`
The condition will always return 0 (false)
Variable y will take the value of x
explanations: Correct! The expression `x = y` assigns 5 to variable `x` and yields 5. By C rules, any non-zero value is true, so the `if` branch executes.
Incorrect. In C, assignment inside conditions is syntactically allowed, although compilers may issue a warning.
Incorrect. The result of the assignment is 5, which is interpreted as true (non-zero).
Incorrect. The `=` operator assigns the right operand's value to the left, so `y`'s value is copied to `x`, not vice versa.

questions.q: Is it true that when reading integers via scanf("%d", &x); you must pass the variable's address (&x) rather than its value (x)?
questions.hint: Think about whether the scanf function can modify an external variable's value if passed only a copy of the value.
options: True
False
explanations: Correct! The `scanf` function must write the read data into the variable's memory, so it requires passing the variable's address via the `&` operator.
Incorrect. Passing `x` instead of `&x` leads to an attempted write to an arbitrary address and a crash (Segmentation Fault).

questions.topic: Branching — Algorithm Behavior with Equal Values
questions.q: How will the algorithm for finding the maximum of two numbers behave if two identical numbers (x = 5, y = 5) are entered as arguments x and y?
questions.hint: Trace the execution of condition x > y when x = 5 and y = 5.
options: Condition 5 > 5 will return 'false', the program will jump to the else branch and print 5 (value of y)
Condition 5 > 5 will return 'true', the program will jump to the if branch and print 5 (value of x)
The program will terminate with a division-by-zero error
The program will enter an infinite loop
explanations: Correct! Since `5 > 5` is false, execution proceeds to the `else` branch, which prints the value of `y` (i.e. 5). The result 5 is the correct maximum.
Incorrect. Strict inequality `5 > 5` yields false, so the `else` branch is selected.
Incorrect. Comparison arithmetic contains no division operations.
Incorrect. `if...else` branching is a one-time check and creates no loops.

questions.topic: Branching — Ternary Operator as an Equivalent to if...else
questions.q: Is it true that an expression with the ternary operator max = (x > y) ? x : y; is completely equivalent to the construct if (x > y) max = x; else max = y;?
questions.hint: Compare how conditions work in the ternary operator and in the if...else construct.
options: True
False
explanations: Correct! The ternary operator `?:` evaluates the condition and returns either the first expression (if true) or the second (if false).
Incorrect. These are conceptually and logically identical forms of branching syntax.

questions.q: Is it true that both branching paths ('true' and 'false') on a selection flowchart converge into a single common flow point before termination (END)?
questions.hint: Think about how algorithm branches merge after executing alternative actions.
options: True
False
explanations: Correct! On a flowchart, after executing their output operations (`x` or `y`), the 'true' and 'false' branches merge into a single control flow leading to the end block.
Incorrect. The flowchart clearly shows the merging of branches before termination.

questions.q: What will the call printf("Maximum: %d", x); output if the value of x is 10?
questions.hint: Recall how the %d specifier substitutes the value of an integer variable.
options: Maximum: 10
Maximum: %d 10
Maximum: x
explanations: Correct! The `%d` specifier inside the format string is replaced by the text representation of the integer from variable `x` (10).
Incorrect. The `%d` specifier is replaced by the value, rather than remaining in the output string.
Incorrect. The text "Maximum: " preceding the specifier will also be printed.
Incorrect. The numeric value of the variable is substituted instead of its name.

questions.q: Is it true that replacing condition if (x > y) with if (!(x <= y)) yields absolutely identical program behavior for any integers?
questions.hint: Apply the laws of logic to strict and non-strict inequalities for integers.
options: True
False
explanations: Correct! Negation of `x <= y` is equivalent to the strict check `x > y` for all integers.
Incorrect. These expressions are logically completely equivalent.

questions.topic: Branching — Behavior When else Branch Is Omitted
questions.q: What will happen during program execution if the else branch is omitted (using only if(condition)) and the tested condition turns out to be false?
questions.hint: Recall how the short form of branching constructs operates.
options: The block of instructions inside if will be skipped, and execution will immediately continue with the instruction following if
The program will terminate with a runtime error
The compiler will generate an error due to the absence of a mandatory else block
The program will enter an infinite waiting loop
explanations: Correct! The `else` branch is optional. If the condition is false, the `if` branch is simply skipped and control passes forward.
Incorrect. Omitting the `else` branch is standard behavior in C.
Incorrect. The `else` branch is optional, so the compiler will not issue an error.
Incorrect. A standalone `if` without `else` does not create loops.

questions.topic: Branching — Finding the Maximum Without an else Branch
questions.q: What will the code snippet in the widget output, where the maximum search algorithm is implemented using a standalone if?
questions.hint: Trace whether the value of variable max changes after checking condition x > y.
options: Compilation error
explanations: Correct! Initially `max` is 20 (`y`). Since condition `10 > 20` is false, the `if` body is skipped, and variable `max` retains the value 20.
Incorrect. The value of `max` would change to 10 only if `x` were strictly greater than `y`.
Incorrect. Variable `max` was initialized to the value of `y` (20), not zero.
Incorrect. The code syntax is correct and will compile without errors.

questions.q: How does the C compiler interpret the result of an expression inside the parentheses of an if (condition) statement?
questions.hint: Recall which numeric values in C are considered true and which are considered false.
options: The value 0 is interpreted as false, and any non-zero value as true
Only positive numbers are considered true, and negative numbers false
The expression must return a boolean type bool from stdbool.h
Inside if, only comparison operators (>, <, ==) are allowed
explanations: Correct! In C, truth value is based on numbers: value `0` corresponds to false, and any non-zero number (including negative ones) is considered true.
Incorrect. Negative numbers are also non-zero, so they are perceived by the compiler as true.
Incorrect. The `bool` type in C appeared later (in C99); historically and syntactically, any integer or floating type can be used as conditions.
Incorrect. Any arithmetic expression or function call returning a number can serve as a condition.

questions.topic: Branching — Syntax Error Binding if and else
questions.q: What will happen when attempting to compile the code snippet shown in the widget?
questions.hint: Pay attention to the presence of statement printf("Y"); between the if branch and else branch when curly braces are absent.
options: The compiler will issue an error because else was separated from if by an intervening statement
The code will compile and output "Y"
The code will compile and output "Z"
The code will compile and output "YZ"
explanations: Correct! Without curly braces, only `printf("X");` belongs to `if`. The next line `printf("Y");` terminates the branching structure, leaving the `else` keyword syntactically orphaned.
Incorrect. The compiler will issue an `error: 'else' without a previous 'if'`.
Incorrect. The code will fail compilation due to an `else` binding syntax error.
Incorrect. The program will not even compile.

questions.topic: Branching — Algorithm Execution Analysis with User Input
questions.q: What will be the result of running the maximum search program if the user inputs values 15 and 20?
questions.hint: Substitute values into scanf: x = 15, y = 20 and evaluate condition x > y.
options: The program will output 20, because the if branch will be skipped and else will execute
The program will output 15
The program will terminate with an error due to invalid number ordering
The program will request user input again
explanations: Correct! Value `x` becomes 15, and `y` becomes 20. Checking `15 > 20` yields false, control passes to `else`, and the program prints `20`.
Incorrect. Condition `15 > 20` is false, so the first `if` branch does not execute.
Incorrect. Input order of numbers does not affect execution; it compares them correctly.
Incorrect. `scanf` executes input once and passes control forward.

questions.q: What will the widget code snippet output if arithmetic expression x - y is passed as the condition in if?
questions.hint: Evaluate expression 5 - 5 and recall how it is interpreted in a condition block.
options: "Same"
"Diff"
Compilation error
Outputs nothing
explanations: Correct! Expression `x - y` gives `5 - 5 = 0`. Number `0` is interpreted in C as false, so the `else` branch executes, printing "Same".
Incorrect. The `if` branch executes only when the expression result is non-zero.
Incorrect. Passing an arithmetic expression to `if` is syntactically valid.
Incorrect. The `else` branch will execute and output "Same".

questions.topic: Branching — Correspondence Between Pseudocode and C Code
questions.q: Which line of C code strictly corresponds to the pseudocode step 'if x>y then print x'?
questions.hint: Find the combination of condition operator and output function for true condition in C code.
options: if(x>y) printf("Maximum: %d", x);
scanf("%d", &x);
else printf("Maximum: %d", y);
main() { int x, y; }
explanations: Correct! The step 'if x>y' translates into `if(x>y)`, and 'then print x' into the print call `printf(..., x)`.
Incorrect. `scanf` corresponds to the pseudocode step 'read x'.
Incorrect. This line corresponds to the step 'else print y'.
Incorrect. This line is a function and variable declaration, not a branching statement.

questions.q: What will the cascading branching structure from the widget output when x = 10?
questions.hint: Check conditions in order: first the first, then the second if the first is false.
options: "BC"
explanations: Correct! First condition `10 < 5` is false. Control moves to `else if`. Second condition `10 < 15` is true, so `printf("B")` executes and the structure completes.
Incorrect. First condition `10 < 5` is not met, and after the first matched `else if` remaining branches are skipped.
Incorrect. Control will not reach the `else` branch (`"C"`) because the `else if` condition matched.
Incorrect. Cascading `if...else if...else` executes only the first true branch, not a combination of several.

questions.q: What is the strict execution sequence of maximum search algorithm steps on a flowchart?
questions.hint: Trace the arrows from the BEGIN block down to the condition check.
options: Input x -> Input y -> Check x > y -> Output result (x or y) -> End (END)
Check x > y -> Input x -> Input y -> END
Input x and y simultaneously -> Output x -> END
Input x -> Check x > y -> Input y -> END
explanations: Correct! The flowchart sets the sequence clearly: first `x` is read, then `y`, followed by branching on `x > y` to output `x` or `y` and algorithm completion.
Incorrect. Comparing variables is impossible before they are read.
Incorrect. Arguments are read first, and outputting `x` depends on the comparison result.
Incorrect. `y` must be read before performing the `x > y` check.

questions.topic: Branching — Pitfall of a Semicolon After if
questions.q: How will the program behave if a semicolon is accidentally placed immediately after an if statement, e.g.: if (x > y); printf("%d", x);?
questions.hint: Think about what a semicolon represents to a C compiler.
options: The semicolon will be parsed as a null statement, so printf will execute always, regardless of condition
The compiler will issue a syntax error
The printf call will never execute
The program will enter an infinite loop
explanations: Correct! Semicolon `;` forms a null statement. Condition `if (x > y);` controls this null statement, and the following `printf` executes always as a separate independent statement.
Incorrect. This is valid C syntax (though often a programmer's logic error).
Incorrect. The `printf` call lies outside the conditional block and executes unconditionally.
Incorrect. A single `if` with a null statement creates no loop.

questions.topic: Branching — Using Curly Braces {} in if Blocks
questions.q: What will happen if multiple statements need to execute inside an if block, but are not enclosed in curly braces {}?
questions.hint: Recall how many statements default to an if operator when curly braces are omitted.
options: Only the first statement will belong to the if branch, while the rest will execute always, regardless of condition
The compiler will automatically group all subsequent statements into one block until the end of the function
The program will compile with a fatal "Missing block braces" error
All statements inside if will be ignored by the compiler
explanations: Correct! If curly braces `{}` are not used to create a compound statement, only the very first statement following `if` belongs to the `if` branch. All subsequent statements execute in standard linear order.
Incorrect. Without `{}` braces, strictly the first statement belongs to the condition.
Incorrect. Curly braces are optional for single-statement `if` branches, so the compiler raises no error.
Incorrect. The first statement binds to `if` rather than being ignored.

questions.topic: Branching — Logical NOT (!) and Checking for Zero
questions.q: What will the code snippet in the widget output when x = 0?
questions.hint: Recall how logical NOT ! inverts the truth value of zero in C.
options: Zero
Not zero
Outputs nothing
Compilation error
explanations: Correct! In C, `0` is considered false. Negation `!0` turns false into true (`1`), so the `if` branch executes and outputs "Zero".
Incorrect. Since `x = 0`, expression `!x` yields true (`1`), directing execution to the first branch.
Incorrect. The first `if` branch will execute and print "Zero".
Incorrect. The code compiles without errors.

questions.q: What will the code snippet in the widget output and what will variable y equal after evaluating the condition?
questions.hint: Think about whether the right side of logical AND (&&) will evaluate if the left side already yields false (0).
options: Outputs 5 (the second expression ++y > 5 was not evaluated)
Outputs 6
Outputs "A6"
Runtime error
explanations: Correct! The `&&` operator uses short-circuiting: since `x != 0` is false (`0 != 0` -> 0), the right side `++y > 5` is not even evaluated. Variable `y` remains equal to 5.
Incorrect. In C with `&&`, if the left operand is 0, the right operand is ignored for optimization.
Incorrect. The `if` condition turns out false, so the branch printing "A" does not execute.
Incorrect. Short-circuiting is standard C behavior causing no runtime errors.

questions.q: How does the evaluation result of condition if (x >= y) differ from if (x > y) when variables are equal (x = 5, y = 5)?
questions.hint: Compare strict vs non-strict inequality when operands are equal.
options: x >= y returns true (1), while x > y returns false (0)
Both conditions return true (1)
Both conditions return false (0)
The expression x >= y causes a syntax error
explanations: Correct! Non-strict inequality `>=` includes equality, so `5 >= 5` is true. Strict inequality `5 > 5` is false.
Incorrect. Strict inequality `>` is not satisfied when values are equal.
Incorrect. Non-strict inequality `>=` is true when values are equal.
Incorrect. `>=` is a standard binary comparison operator in C.

questions.topic: Branching — Behavior of Nested if Conditions Without else
questions.q: What will the program in the widget output with values a = 5 and b = 10?
questions.hint: Trace step by step: is the first condition met? Is the second condition met?
options: Outputs nothing
Compilation error
explanations: Correct! First condition `a > 0` (5 > 0) is true, so the program enters the inner `if`. There `b < 5` (10 < 5) is checked — it is false, so its associated `else` branch executes, printing "2".
Incorrect. Nested condition `b < 5` is false, so its `else` block executes.
Incorrect. The nested `else` branch will execute and print "2".
Incorrect. The code contains no syntax errors.

questions.q: In which case will the compound expression (a > 0 || b > 0) return false (0)?
questions.hint: Recall the truth table for the logical OR operator.
options: Only when both a <= 0 and b <= 0 simultaneously
When at least one variable is less than or equal to 0
When a <= 0, but b > 0
This expression is always true
explanations: Correct! The `||` operator yields false (`0`) only when **both** of its operands are simultaneously false.
Incorrect. If at least one operand is true, `||` returns true (`1`).
Incorrect. If `b > 0`, the right operand is true, hence the entire `||` expression is true.
Incorrect. The expression can be false if both conditions are false.

questions.q: What advantage does writing if (5 == x) offer compared to standard if (x == 5)?
questions.hint: Think about what happens if a developer typos single = instead of double ==.
options: An accidental typo if (5 = x) triggers a compilation error, preventing accidental assignment
Such code runs twice as fast at the hardware level
Writing 5 == x allows floating-point comparison without loss of precision
This is the only valid syntax adopted in C99 standard
explanations: Correct! Accidental `if (x = 5)` executes assignment in C. But `if (5 = x)` causes a compiler error because a value cannot be assigned to literal `5`.
Incorrect. This style does not affect execution speed or standard compliance; its goal is preventing typo bugs.
Incorrect. Yoda conditions do not affect floating-point comparison precision.
Incorrect. Both operand orders (`x == 5` and `5 == x`) fully conform to C standards.

questions.q: Is it true that any algorithm with if...else branching can always be rewritten using only standalone if constructs without using else?
questions.hint: Think about whether else can be replaced by a second if with an inverted condition.
options: True
False
explanations: Correct! The `else` branch can always be logically replaced by a separate `if` statement with an inverted condition, though it might reduce code readability.
Incorrect. Structurally, `else` is not a strictly mandatory language element.

questions.topic: Branching — Postfix Increment in a Condition
questions.q: What will the code in the widget output with initial value x = 3?
questions.hint: Recall the difference between postfix (x++) and prefix (++x) increment when evaluating a condition.
options: A
B
AB
Compilation error
explanations: Correct! Postfix increment `x++` first returns the current value (3), which is interpreted as true, and then increments `x` to 4. Therefore, the `if` branch executes and prints "A".
Incorrect. Since initial `x = 3` is non-zero, the condition is true.
Incorrect. Only one `if` branch executes, printing "A".
Incorrect. Syntactically, postfix increment inside `if` is completely legal.

questions.q: Which of the following statements most accurately describes the purpose of a selection (branching) control construct in C?
questions.hint: Think about how branching alters sequential program execution.
options: Allows altering the execution order of instructions depending on condition truth
Allows repeatedly executing a block of instructions a specified number of times
Allows dynamically allocating RAM memory
Serves exclusively for keyboard user input
explanations: Correct! Selection (branching) control structures allow a program to deviate from strict sequential instruction execution and choose alternative code paths based on conditions.
Incorrect. Repeating blocks is the task of loops, not branching.
Incorrect. Memory allocation is performed by functions like `malloc`.
Incorrect. Data input is performed using functions like `scanf`.
